Finding your way through the forest of available semiliquid private credit vehicles remains daunting, even though fund-level Securities and Exchange Commission filings leave some breadcrumbs—such as names, descriptions of the interest rates on their loans, and other notes—and managers usually release some aggregated statistics.

Those are scraps, however, compared with what traditional mutual and exchange-traded funds report, making it hard for investors to evaluate how much risk they are taking or whether their portfolios are under stress.
For example, a nontraded business-development company that can borrow $1 for every dollar of investors’ money offers around 200% of the market exposure the investment would otherwise have.
Infrequently updated private credit prices have the potential to produce uneven results for investors.

Meanwhile, if a lot of investors sell when prices are frothy, forcing the fund to mark its loans down to prices that better reflect the portfolio’s risks, it can bite fund shareholders who stick around.
Many private credit managers have assured shareholders that their funds can handle that pressure because they have plenty of liquidity to meet ongoing requests.
